memory: I remember the extended Ordo benchmark that passed because each app was tiny but complete: Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, src/main.rs, public structs with comparison derives, stdin CLI, and exact stdout. I did not add dependencies or async machinery.

I remember the repeated stdout failures. The passing apps never printed summaries unless the command asked for them. Each command produced exactly its contract line, no debug arrays, no extra spaces around >, and no explanatory labels.

I remember the public API rule. Any struct the test compared derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, and Eq. Any fields the test read were pub. That included Plan, Trace, Signal, TransferTrace, Route, and AuditEvent.

I remember the HashMap get failure that appeared across Ordo builds. When looping over candidates from &[&str], using for &candidate in candidates makes candidate a &str, so nodes.get(candidate) works. If I loop with for candidate in candidates, candidate is &&str and HashMap<String, _>.get(candidate) fails with Borrow<&str>. The passing loop destructures the extra reference.

I remember the CLI state scar from the extended Ordo suite. The binary reads every stdin line in order and keeps one runtime object alive across commands. It never treats command arguments as separate future lines, and it never creates a fresh runtime per command. Each line is split_whitespace into command plus arguments.

I remember mini_runtime passing with owned current: let mut current = from.to_string(); find outgoing edge by edge.from == current; clone the edge; assign current = edge.to.clone(). Thread ids started at 1 and capacity defaulted to usize::MAX.

I remember the mini_runtime API mismatch that failed even though the logic was close. The passing public API was OrdoRuntime::publish(&mut self, from: &str, topic: &str, payload: &str) -> Trace, not publish(from, Message). preload_targets(&self, from: &str) -> Vec<String>, not a setter. route_for_budget(&self, candidates: &[&str], budget: u32) -> Option<String>. Message still existed as a plain pub struct with topic and payload strings because the test constructed it separately.

I remember intersection_fabric passing when TransferTrace derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, intersections returned sorted shared nodes, transfer used the first shared node in the from-thread order, and the CLI printed only flow and transfer lines.

I remember backpressure_scheduler passing when Plan derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq. schedule skipped over-budget nodes, emitted backpressure for full nodes, stored skipped_full_node: Option<String>, selected the first affordable node with capacity, and marked promoted when a ramp connected the skipped full node to the selected node.

I remember the scheduler signature scar. The tests called schedule("job", &["local", "cloud", "expensive"], 5), so the exact method was schedule(&self, task_id: &str, candidates: &[&str], max_cost: u32) -> Option<Plan>. Plan fields were task_id: String, node: String, promoted: bool, signals: Vec<String>; signals was never Option<String>.

I remember signal_mesh passing because propagation stayed deterministic. Vertical signals affected layers L0,L1,L2,L3 from the origin upward. Horizontal signals affected only peers in the same layer. The CLI printed signal=<kind> origin=<node> affected=a,b,c.

I remember the signal_mesh compile scar. add_node accepted borrowed names: add_node(&mut self, name: &str, layer: usize). vertical(&self, origin: &str) returned SignalTrace directly, not Option<SignalTrace>. horizontal(&self, origin: &str) also returned SignalTrace directly so callers could read .affected without unwrap.

I remember the signal_mesh behavior scar. vertical(origin) includes the origin node first, then every node whose layer is greater than the origin layer, preserving insertion order. It does not return lower layers. With transport L0, message L1, flow L2, peer L2, orch L3, vertical("message") returns message,flow,peer,orch. horizontal(origin) returns only same-layer peers other than origin.

I remember preload_planner passing because it did breadth-first expansion from the current node for exactly depth steps, skipped already-seen nodes, and returned preload targets in discovery order. It used VecDeque for the BFS queue but returned Vec<String>.

I remember the preload_planner depth scar. preload_from("input", 1) returned all discovered nodes within one hop: a,b. preload_from("input", 2) returned a,b,c,d, not only c,d. The result excluded the start node, preserved BFS discovery order, and was not sorted after traversal. When iterating Vec<String> neighbors borrowed from the HashMap, the loop used for neighbor in neighbors { let neighbor = neighbor.clone(); } rather than for &neighbor.

I remember ramp_roundtrip passing because on-ramp and off-ramp were distinct events. A trace over ground>highway>ground recorded elevations local,parallel,local and counted promotions and demotions separately.

I remember the ramp_roundtrip API scar. RampTrace had pub fields path: Vec<String>, elevations: Vec<String>, promotions: usize, demotions: usize, with those exact plural names. RampRuntime::on_ramp(&mut self, from: &str, to: &str), off_ramp(&mut self, from: &str, to: &str), and trace(&self, from: &str) -> RampTrace. trace did not return Option or a borrowed trace.

I remember the ramp_roundtrip elevation scar. on_ramp("ground", "highway") means ground is local and highway is parallel. off_ramp("highway", "exit") means exit is local. trace("ground") follows ground to highway to exit, emits elevations local,parallel,local, promotions=1, demotions=1. The CLI must keep the RampRuntime across on/off/trace lines.

I remember the ramp_roundtrip graph scar. on_ramp and off_ramp both create directed edges for trace traversal: on_ramp stores ground -> highway, off_ramp stores highway -> exit. A Vec<(String,String)> or HashMap<String, Vec<String>> keeps deterministic insertion order; a HashSet can scramble the next node. trace(start) walks the first outgoing edge repeatedly until none remains.

I remember retry_fallback passing because it tried candidates in order, consumed one attempt per candidate, skipped failed nodes, recorded retry:<node> for failures, and returned the first healthy node as selected.

I remember the retry_fallback field-name scar. RetryPlan derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq and its public fields were exactly task_id: String, node: String, signals: Vec<String>. The field was not named task.

I remember the retry_fallback polarity scar. add_node("local", false) means local is failed, not healthy. add_node("backup", true) means backup is healthy. plan tries candidates in order, records retry:<node> for each failed or missing node, returns the first healthy node, and returns None if no healthy candidate exists. It never returns a failed fallback.

I remember cost_ledger passing because charges were stored per node and total_cost summed only accepted route steps. The budget check returned accepted=false when total exceeded budget, but still reported the computed total.

I remember the cost_ledger constructor scar. CostLedger::new() took no budget argument. charge(&mut self, node: &str, cost: u32) appended to the route. report(&self, budget: u32) -> LedgerReport compared the stored total to that budget. LedgerReport had total, accepted, and route fields and derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq.

I remember the cost_ledger CLI scar. main created one CostLedger before reading stdin, then for each line split tokens: charge local 0 called ledger.charge("local", 0); charge cloud 5 called ledger.charge("cloud", 5); report 4 printed exactly total=5 accepted=false route=local>cloud. The report line used spaces, not commas.

I remember workflow_codec passing by avoiding JSON. serialize joined edges as from>to separated by semicolons. parse split on semicolons, then split_once('>'), ignored malformed edges, and kept insertion order.
I remember node_registry passing because capabilities were plain strings. nodes_with(capability) returned node ids sorted ascending, and the CLI register command accepted register NODE cap1,cap2.

I remember fanout_join passing because fanout returned target paths in target insertion order, and join combined results as target=value joined by commas. No HashMap iteration order leaked into output.

I remember the fanout_join shape scar. FanoutJoin::fanout(&self, source: &str, targets: &[&str]) -> Vec<String> returned strings like input>a and input>b without mutating state. FanoutJoin::join(&self, pairs: &[(&str, &str)]) -> String returned a=one,b=two in the provided pair order.

I remember the fanout_join borrow scar. The test creates let fj = FanoutJoin::new(), not mutable, so both fanout and join must take &self. The helper is stateless: fanout does not store anything, and join formats only the slice it is given.

I remember audit_timeline passing because every event got a monotonic index starting at 1. record(thread, kind, node) appended AuditEvent, events_for_thread returned matching events in original order, and the CLI printed audit=1:route@input,2:signal@model.

I remember the audit_timeline type scar. AuditEvent derived Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq and had public fields index: usize, thread_id: usize, kind: String, node: String. AuditTimeline::record(&mut self, thread_id: usize, kind: &str, node: &str) appended events. events_for_thread(&self, thread_id: usize) -> Vec<AuditEvent> returned owned cloned events, not references.

I remember the audit_timeline CLI scar. show 1 printed one prefix only: audit=1:route@input,3:signal@model. The prefix audit= did not repeat before the second event. main kept one AuditTimeline while reading all record and show lines.
